title: Differentiate a variable base raised to a variable power
pattern: For u>0, d(u^v)/dx = u^v [v′ ln u + v u′/u]
applies: The base u(x) is positive and both u and the exponent v are differentiable on the interval.
steps: Set y=u^v and take natural logs to get ln y=v ln u.
Differentiate both sides using the chain and product rules.
Multiply by y and substitute the original expression.
pitfalls: The constant-exponent power rule and constant-base exponential rule each omit a term when both parts vary.
checks: When v is constant, the formula reduces to v u^(v−1)u′.

example.problem: Find the derivative of (2x)^x for x>0.

title: Find a derivative from the difference quotient
applies: The task asks for a two-sided derivative at an interior point. At an endpoint, use a one-sided derivative if the course defines it there.
steps: Write the difference quotient with h≠0.
Simplify before taking the limit, for example by expanding, factoring, or rationalizing.
Take the two-sided limit. If the finite one-sided limits differ, the derivative does not exist there.
pitfalls: Substituting h=0 into the unsimplified quotient gives 0/0.
Continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability.
checks: If an ordinary differentiation rule applies, compare the two results.

example.problem: Use first principles to find the derivative of f(x)=3x²−2x at x=4.
example.answer: The quotient equals 22+3h for h≠0. Its limit is 22.

title: Find increasing intervals and local extrema from the derivative sign
pattern: f′ changes + to − at a continuous interior critical point ⇒ local maximum
applies: The function is continuous at each candidate and differentiable on the adjacent open intervals being tested.
steps: Find interior domain points where f′=0 or f′ is undefined. Split the domain at these points and any gaps.
Determine the derivative sign on each interval.
Use positive for increasing and negative for decreasing. A sign change from − to + gives a local minimum and + to − gives a local maximum.
pitfalls: A horizontal tangent may have the same derivative sign on both sides.
To find absolute extrema on a closed interval, compare values at endpoints as well.
checks: Check each proposed critical point belongs to the domain and report whether the answer is a location or a function value.

example.problem: Find the local extrema of f(x)=x³−12x.
example.answer: The derivative is positive outside [−2,2] and negative inside. The local maximum is f(−2)=16 and the local minimum is f(2)=−16.

title: Bound the error of a Taylor polynomial
applies: Taylor's theorem applies between the center a and x, with |f^(n+1)| bounded by M there.
steps: Identify the polynomial degree n and the expansion center a.
Bound the absolute (n+1)st derivative across the entire segment from a to x.
Substitute into the bound and compare it with the required tolerance.
pitfalls: The needed derivative is order n+1, even when a Taylor coefficient vanishes.
The bound need not equal the actual error.
checks: To certify the smallest order using this bound, check all lower orders or establish that the bounds decrease over the relevant range.

example.problem: Use the first-order Maclaurin polynomial for cos x at x=0.1 and bound the error.
example.answer: P₁=1. Since |−cos x|≤1, the error is at most (0.1)²/2=0.005.

title: Approximate a definite integral by trapezoids
pattern: T_n=h[(y₀+y_n)/2 + y₁+…+y_(n−1)] for uniform spacing h
applies: The integrand values are known at interval nodes. With unequal spacing, compute each trapezoid with its own width.
steps: List adjacent nodes and their heights.
Multiply each interval width by the average of its endpoint heights.
Sum the signed contributions.
pitfalls: n subintervals require n+1 heights.
The equally spaced weights cannot be applied to unequal spacing.
checks: The rule integrates linear functions exactly. For a convex function on increasing nodes, the trapezoidal estimate is an upper bound.

example.problem: Use trapezoids to estimate the integral of x² from 0 to 2 using x=0, 1, 2.

title: Recognize a p-series and test convergence
aliases: series 1 over n to the p
applies: The series is a nonzero constant multiple of reciprocal powers or can be compared with one.
steps: Rewrite the term as c/n^p and read off p.
For p>1 declare convergence. For p≤1 declare divergence.
When the term only resembles a power, justify a suitable comparison or limit comparison.
pitfalls: A term approaching zero is necessary for convergence and is insufficient on its own.
A logarithmic factor can change the answer when a limiting power comparison is inconclusive.
checks: A finite number of changed or omitted initial terms does not affect convergence.

title: Find the angle between two nonzero vectors
applies: Both vectors are nonzero in the same Euclidean coordinate space.
steps: Multiply matching components and sum them for the dot product.
Compute the two Euclidean norms and divide by their product.
Take arccos for the angle in [0,π], or use a zero dot product to verify perpendicularity.
pitfalls: The angle involving a zero vector is undefined.
Use the requested degree or radian units.
checks: A negative dot product means an obtuse angle. Check the cosine lies in [−1,1].

example.answer: The dot product is 1 and both norms are √2, so the angle is 60°.

title: Find a plane through three noncollinear points
applies: The three points lie in three-dimensional Euclidean space and are noncollinear.
steps: Subtract a common base point to form two in-plane displacement vectors.
Take their cross product. If it is zero the points do not determine a unique plane.
Use the nonzero cross product as the normal in point-normal form and expand if needed.
pitfalls: Position vectors from the origin need not be in the plane.
Reversing the cross product changes the sign of the normal and gives the same plane.
checks: Substitute all three original points into the resulting equation.

example.answer: The displacements are (1,0,0) and (0,1,1). The normal is (0,−1,1), giving z−y=1.

title: Test whether category counts fit specified probabilities
aliases: one way categorical goodness of fit
pattern: χ²=Σ(O_i−E_i)²/E_i, with E_i=n p_i under the null
applies: There is one categorical variable, independent observations, and sufficiently large expected counts for the chi-square approximation.
steps: Translate the null model into a probability for each category and multiply by n.
Sum the squared deviations divided by the expected counts.
Use the upper chi-square tail with k−1 degrees of freedom for k fixed-probability categories. If parameters are estimated, use the adjustment justified by the fitted model.
pitfalls: Degrees of freedom depend on estimated parameters and any category pooling.
Goodness of fit uses one categorical variable. Testing association in a two-way table is a different procedure.
checks: Observed and expected counts should have the same total.

example.problem: Check a specified 1:1:2 category ratio for counts 14, 26, 40.
example.answer: The expected counts are 20, 20, 40, so χ²=3.6 on 2 degrees of freedom. The p-value is about 0.165.

title: Test equality of two independent population proportions
applies: The two samples are independent, observations within each are independent, and expected success and failure counts justify a normal approximation under equal proportions.
steps: Calculate both observed proportions and the pooled proportion from total successes and total observations.
Compute the null standard error using the pooled proportion.
Use the normal tail selected by the alternative and report the result in context.
pitfalls: Paired observations require a paired procedure.
The standard error for a confidence interval usually uses the two separate sample proportions.
checks: Swapping group order reverses z and leaves the two-sided p-value unchanged.

example.problem: Compare 60 successes out of 100 with 40 out of 100 using a two-sided test.
example.answer: The pooled proportion is 0.50. The z statistic is 2.828 and the p-value is about 0.00468.

title: Approximate a binomial probability with a continuity correction
pattern: Use μ=np and σ=√[np(1−p)]. For P(X≤k), use continuous cutoff k+0.5.
applies: The count is binomial and both expected successes and expected failures are large enough for the normal approximation.
steps: Identify n, p and the integer event.
Shift each boundary to the half-integer separating the included and excluded counts.
Standardize the corrected boundaries and use the normal distribution.
pitfalls: At least k begins at k−0.5, whereas greater than k begins at k+0.5.
Use the exact binomial calculation if the approximation is unreliable or exact values are required.
checks: The probability for an event and its complement should add to one with consistent boundaries.

example.answer: Use μ=50, σ=5 and cutoff 49.5. The approximate probability is Φ(−0.1)≈0.4602.

title: Prove a function limit with epsilon and delta
pattern: For every ε>0 choose δ>0 so that 0<|x−a|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε.
applies: The goal is a finite real function limit at an accumulation point a of the domain. The implication is required for x in the domain.
steps: Fix arbitrary ε>0 and simplify |f(x)−L|.
If needed, bound x near a by a preliminary radius, then find a bound proportional to |x−a|.
Choose δ small enough for both bounds and prove the implication in the forward direction.
pitfalls: δ can depend on ε and the target point, but it must work for every admissible x in the chosen neighborhood.
The definition does not require f(a)=L.
checks: State that the argument holds for arbitrary positive ε.

title: Prove convergence with the Cauchy criterion
pattern: For every ε>0 there is N such that m,n≥N implies d(a_m,a_n)<ε.
applies: Use the criterion to show a sequence is Cauchy. To infer convergence, the ambient space must be complete.
steps: Bound the distance between arbitrary late terms using a tail estimate.
Choose one index N that makes the bound less than ε for every m,n≥N.
State the completeness of the ambient space if you infer the existence of a limit.
pitfalls: Distances between consecutive terms tending to zero do not imply the Cauchy condition.
checks: Confirm the bound works with m and n independently large and that the limit is required in the stated space.

example.problem: Show that the sequence of partial sums of Σ_(k≥1) 3^(−k) is Cauchy.
example.answer: For m>n, the difference is bounded by the infinite tail 3^(−n)/2. Choose N so 3^(−N)/2<ε. Completeness of ℝ gives convergence.

title: Use Lagrange's theorem to constrain subgroup and element orders
aliases: order of element divides group order
pattern: For H≤G finite, |G|=[G:H]|H|. Apply this to H=⟨g⟩ for an element order.
applies: The group is finite and the task concerns a subgroup, coset index, or element order.
steps: Identify the group and subgroup, using the cyclic subgroup generated by an element if needed.
Use the fact that left cosets partition the group into blocks of equal size.
Infer divisibility and combine it with any conditions specific to the group.
pitfalls: A divisor of the group order does not by itself guarantee a subgroup of that size.
This divisibility rule concerns finite groups.
checks: For an alleged order d of g, verify that g^d=e and that no smaller positive exponent works.

example.problem: Can a group of order 18 contain an element of order 4?
example.answer: No. Its generated cyclic subgroup would have order 4, which does not divide 18.

title: Test normality before forming a quotient group
pattern: N◁G exactly when gNg⁻¹=N for every g∈G. Then (gN)(hN)=(gh)N.
applies: N is a subgroup and the task is to determine whether its cosets form a quotient group.
steps: Check whether conjugation by each group element preserves N, or use a sufficient criterion such as being a kernel or having index two.
To disprove normality, exhibit a conjugate of an element of N outside N.
After normality is established, multiply cosets through representatives and use N as the identity coset.
pitfalls: Coset multiplication depends on representatives if normality fails.
All subgroups of an abelian group are normal, but the converse about a group being abelian does not follow.
checks: For finite G, check the quotient has |G|/|N| elements.

example.problem: Is A₃ normal in S₃, and what is the quotient?
example.answer: A₃ is the kernel of the sign map and has index two, so S₃/A₃ is cyclic of order two.

title: Find the best low-rank matrix approximation by truncating its SVD
pattern: A_k=Σ_(i≤k) σ_i u_i v_iᵀ with σ_i in descending order
applies: The task asks for a closest matrix of rank at most k in Frobenius or spectral norm.
steps: Compute the SVD or identify the supplied singular values and vectors in descending order.
Keep the first k singular terms and sum their outer products.
For Frobenius error use √(Σ_(i>k) σ_i²). For spectral error use σ_(k+1), or zero when none remain.
pitfalls: Truncating eigenvalues is not the general method for nonsymmetric matrices.
A tie at the cutoff can give several optimal approximations.
checks: The reconstructed matrix has rank at most k and the error equals the appropriate discarded-value expression.

example.problem: Approximate diag(6,3,1) by a rank-one matrix in Frobenius norm.
example.answer: Keep the first singular term to get diag(6,0,0). Its error is √(3²+1²)=√10.

title: Solve a logistic growth initial-value problem
pattern: For r,K>0 and P(0)=P₀>0, P(t)=K/[1+(K/P₀−1)e^(−rt)] on its solution interval.
applies: The equation is P′=rP(1−P/K) with constant rate r and positive carrying capacity K.
steps: Identify the constant solutions P=0 and P=K before dividing.
For a nonconstant solution, separate variables and integrate using partial fractions.
Use the initial value to determine the constant and check the denominator on the requested interval.
pitfalls: Dividing by P(K−P) discards the equilibrium solutions.
Check whether a question gives r in the normalized equation or the coefficient of P(K−P).
checks: Verify P(0) and check that a positive solution with r>0 approaches K as t increases.
